message.content: No, not in standard probability. A finite expectation means the variable is integrable. That is, its absolute value has finite expectation. This condition is stronger than mere conditional summability. For discrete variables, it implies an absolutely convergent sum. If X and Y both have finite expectations, then both are integrable. The sum of two integrable random variables is integrable. The triangle inequality proves this directly. We have |X + Y| ≤ |X| + |Y|. Taking expectations preserves the inequality. Hence E(|X + Y|) ≤ E(|X|) + E(|Y|). The right side is finite by assumption. Therefore E(|X + Y|) is finite. So E(X + Y) exists and is finite. It cannot be undefined or infinite. Linearity also gives E(X + Y) = E(X) + E(Y). No independence assumption is needed. No normality or symmetry assumption is needed. A deceptive example would have to hide infinite tails. But an infinite tail makes the individual mean not finite. Thus the assumptions already exclude such a construction. The answer to the reference text is therefore no. Even after carefully checking the positive and negative parts of both variables and after verifying that each marginal expectation is genuinely finite in the usual Lebesgue sense one finds no real valid counterexample beneath the surface of the question.
